title: Snowflake governance and cost
summary: Role design, masking and row access policies, tags, lineage and access history, and the levers that control and attribute Snowflake spend.

blocks.text: Governance and cost share the same tools: roles, tags and the `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE` views. Several features here (masking, row access policies, access history) require Enterprise edition or higher; check your edition.
29.1 Role-based access control

In Snowflake, privileges are granted to **roles**, and roles are granted to users and to other roles. A user acts through a primary role (plus secondary roles if enabled), and inherits everything granted to roles below it in the hierarchy. Every object has an owning role.

blocks.title: A common role hierarchy

layers.label: SYSADMIN
layers.sub: owns custom role tree, databases, warehouses

blocks.caption: Grant custom roles up to SYSADMIN so administrators can manage what they create.

blocks.text: The usual pattern separates **access roles**, which hold privileges on objects (read-only or read-write on one database or schema), from **functional roles**, which represent jobs and are granted a set of access roles. Users get functional roles only. Changing what a job may see means changing grants between roles, not touching users.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: access and functional roles

blocks.text: Use **managed access schemas** for governed data: only the schema owner or a role with MANAGE GRANTS can grant access to its objects, keeping grants centralized.
29.2 Masking and row access policies
Policies are schema-level objects attached to columns or tables and evaluated at query time for every query, whatever tool issues it.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: column masking and row filtering

items: `IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION` respects role hierarchy and secondary roles; `CURRENT_ROLE()` checks only the primary role, which is simpler but stricter.
A mapping table for row access keeps entitlements as data, so adding a region to a role is an INSERT, not a policy change.

blocks.text: Tags and tag-based masking

A **tag** is a schema-level object you set on accounts, warehouses, databases, tables or columns with a string value. Tags drive classification (`pii = 'email'`), cost attribution (`cost_center = 'marketing'`) and policy. Assign a masking policy to a tag, and every column carrying that tag is masked by it automatically (one policy per data type per tag), including columns added later.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: tag-based masking

blocks.text: 29.3 Lineage and audit

head: View (SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE)
Answers
rows: Who read or wrote which tables and columns, per query, including base objects behind views
Which views and other objects depend on which tables (impact analysis before a change)
Which policies are attached to which objects
What ran, by whom, how long, on which warehouse; who logged in from where

blocks.text: These views lag by minutes to a few hours and keep about a year of history; `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` functions are near real-time but shorter-lived. Copy what compliance needs into your own tables.
29.4 Where credits go

items: **Warehouses**: per-second credits after a 60-second minimum per resume; usually the largest share.

**Serverless features**: Snowpipe, automatic clustering, search optimization, materialized view and Dynamic Table maintenance where serverless, serverless tasks, query acceleration. Each has its own rate and usage view.
**Cloud services**: billed only above a daily allowance; matters for very frequent tiny queries.
**Storage**: compressed bytes per month, including time travel and fail-safe. High-churn tables with long retention can store several times their live size.
**Data transfer**: egress across regions or clouds.

blocks.text: 29.5 Controlling spend

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: guardrails
blocks.text:
ALTER WAREHOUSE transform_wh SET
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 3600;

CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR rm_transform WITH
  CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
           ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;

ALTER WAREHOUSE transform_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = rm_transform;

items: **Auto-suspend** of about 60 seconds suits batch warehouses; BI warehouses may justify a few minutes to keep their cache (chapter 26).
**Resource monitors** cap warehouse credits per period and can notify or suspend. They do not cover serverless features; use **budgets** for broader spend alerts.
**Statement timeouts** stop runaway queries from burning a warehouse for hours.

**Query acceleration** (`ENABLE_QUERY_ACCELERATION`, with a max scale factor) offloads parts of large scans to serverless compute. It suits occasional outlier queries better than permanent upsizing. `SYSTEM$ESTIMATE_QUERY_ACCELERATION` shows whether a past query would have benefited.
**Right-size by evidence**: compare runtime, queuing and spilling in `QUERY_HISTORY` around a resize; one size up should roughly halve parallel runtime.

blocks.text: A dashboard refreshing every minute against a warehouse with a 10-minute auto-suspend keeps that warehouse running 24 hours a day. Many surprise bills come from schedules, not from heavy queries.
29.6 Cost attribution

Attribution answers 'which team or product spent this?'. Put dedicated warehouses per workload where practical and tag them with `cost_center`; for shared warehouses, set `QUERY_TAG` in each tool's session (dbt, Airflow, BI) and allocate compute per query. Snowflake provides per-query compute attribution in ACCOUNT_USAGE (for example `QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY`; check the current documentation for its coverage, which excludes idle time).

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: monthly credits by cost center tag
blocks.text:
SELECT tr.tag_value AS cost_center,
       SUM(m.credits_used) AS credits
FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history m
JOIN snowflake.account_usage.tag_references tr
  ON tr.domain = 'WAREHOUSE'
 AND tr.object_name = m.warehouse_name
 AND tr.tag_name = 'COST_CENTER'
WHERE m.start_time >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY credits DESC;

blocks.title: Halving a bill without slowing anyone down
blocks.text: A platform team found 38% of credits came from three warehouses idling between small queries, and 20% from a full-refresh Dynamic Table with a 1-minute lag read hourly. Shorter auto-suspend on batch warehouses, one multi-cluster BI warehouse, a 1-hour lag, resource monitors and team tags cut monthly spend by about half.

blocks.title: Design governance and cost controls for a new domain
blocks.text: A marketing domain is onboarding: 30 analysts, two data engineers, one BI tool service account, and a customer table with email, phone and country. EU analysts may only see EU customers; only a small group may see unmasked contact data. Design the roles (functional and access), policies and tags, then the warehouses, monitors and attribution so marketing's spend is visible and capped.
hints: Which grants change when an analyst moves from EU to US?
Which column-level controls should follow tags rather than column names?
Which spend would a resource monitor not catch?

items: Grant privileges to access roles, access roles to functional roles, functional roles to users; roll custom roles up to SYSADMIN.
Masking and row access policies apply at query time to every tool; entitlement tables keep them data-driven.
Tags classify objects, attach masking policies to many columns at once and drive cost attribution.
ACCOUNT_USAGE views (access history, object dependencies, query history) provide audit and lineage.
Credits come from warehouses, serverless features and cloud services; storage includes time travel and fail-safe.
Auto-suspend, resource monitors, budgets, timeouts, query acceleration and tagging keep spend controlled and attributable.

blocks.q: Where should SELECT privileges on a sales schema normally be granted in a functional/access role design?
options: To an access role such as SALES_RO, which is then granted to functional roles
To ACCOUNTADMIN, which all users inherit
blocks.explain: Access roles hold object privileges and functional roles bundle them for a job. Granting to users does not scale, and ACCOUNTADMIN or PUBLIC would expose data far too broadly.

blocks.q: A new `contact_email` column is added and tagged `pii = 'email'`. The pii tag has a STRING masking policy. What happens?
options: Nothing until someone attaches the policy to the new column
The tag value is shown instead of the email
The column is masked automatically by the tag's policy
The column is dropped for non-privileged roles
blocks.explain: Tag-based masking applies the tag's policy to every column of the matching data type that carries the tag, including new ones, which is why it scales better than per-column policies.

blocks.q: A resource monitor with a 500-credit monthly quota is attached to every warehouse, yet spend exceeds the plan. Which spend could it have missed?
options: Queries served from the warehouse cache
Queries run by ACCOUNTADMIN on monitored warehouses
Serverless features such as Snowpipe, automatic clustering and serverless tasks
blocks.explain: Resource monitors track warehouses only. Serverless features bill separately and need budgets or usage-view alerts. Scale-out clusters of a monitored warehouse are counted.

blocks.q: Which statement about ACCESS_HISTORY is correct?
options: It records which tables and columns each query read or modified, including base tables behind views
It requires a masking policy on each table
It only records writes, not reads
It is real-time and kept for 7 days
blocks.explain: ACCESS_HISTORY records both reads and writes at column level and resolves views to base objects. ACCOUNT_USAGE views have some latency and long retention.
